title: Leap
hook: The prettiest boot rack in the hotel lobby still rests on one unproved bet.
counterintuition: Listing assumptions looks responsible; the hidden cost is letting the dangerous one stay protected unless the first test targets the belief that could break the plan.
tryThisNow: Choose one project and write the assumption that could break it. Put a star beside that line and design the next test around only that risk.
keyTakeaway: Name the leap your plan depends on, rank it by damage if false, and test the business-breaking assumption first.

breakdown.fastRead:
Laura's boot rack looks perfect beside the ski-town hotel door. The rental tags are crisp. The hotel desk card is clear. The deposit amount has been debated for an hour.

One belief carries the whole plan: tourists will rent winter boots instead of buying them.

The leap is the belief holding the plan up before proof has arrived. Smaller questions can wait. If tourists will not rent, better signage and cleaner tags do not save the model. The riskiest assumption deserves the first test because it decides whether the rest of the work matters.
breakdown.deepRead:
"Trust goes in the top slot," Etienne says while a calendar alert hovers over a tax folder. The fintech team wants to build bank-link integrations for freelancer tax reminders. The bank-link mockup looks impressive. The manual reminder can test the risk sooner: will freelancers trust an automated nudge about taxes before connecting an account?

Leap-of-faith assumptions are the load-bearing beliefs the plan quietly stands on while the team still lacks proof.

Every uncertain project has many assumptions. Some are annoying if false. Some are fatal. The work begins when the team ranks the difference. Menu preferences matter for a meal service, but payer commitment may matter more. Training videos matter for safety education, but supervisor release may matter first. Clause automation matters for legal tools, but client willingness to pay for human review may determine whether automation is valuable at all.

The value hypothesis and growth hypothesis often contain the biggest leaps. Do people care enough to use or pay? Can the business find more of them in a repeatable way? Those questions steer because they sit under everything else.

Polish should not arrive before the floor is tested.
breakdown.fullRead:
Emily clips a sample menu to a fridge magnet and studies the payer call list. The meals have been tested for nutrition, the packaging looks gentle, and families say variety matters. The monthly price is the heavier question. If adult children will not pay every month, the menu debate is decoration.

She calls five payers before approving another recipe cycle.

Riskiest assumption first is the rule: the first test belongs to the assumption that would make every polished detail irrelevant if it failed. That sounds obvious until a team is close to the work. People naturally drift toward assumptions they know how to improve: copy, features, colors, schedules, menu choices, video quality. The lethal assumption often feels rude to test because it threatens the whole project.

What is the belief you keep improving around?

Pavel sees the same pattern at a manufacturing plant. The HR team wants to film safety micro-training modules, but the punch clock and shift roster point to a deeper risk. Supervisors may not release workers for five minutes. The training tablet can be perfect and still sit unused. Pavel tests the release slip before filming, because access to five minutes is the business-breaking assumption for that version of the program.

Assumption ranking is not pessimism. It is steering. A team cannot steer with twenty equal worries. It needs to know which belief gets tested first, which can wait, and which is already known well enough for now. The danger is turning the assumption list into paperwork: a table filled out once, admired for its completeness, and ignored while the team builds around the scariest line.

Maja learns this with a childcare swap. The matching features are easy to imagine. The harder leap is trust. At her kitchen table, printed emergency contacts and a two-family cap sit beside a trial evening form. In the postmortem, she names reciprocal care as the real leap and asks two families to try one evening before building a matching system. The small test may feel humble, but it touches the load-bearing belief.

There is a limit to fear-based ranking. If every assumption is called fatal, the team freezes. The ranking has to be practical: which false belief would make the current plan collapse or change shape dramatically? Test that one. If it survives, move to the next. If it fails, be grateful that it failed while the cost was still small.

Jack faces the question with a legal-document automation tool. A marked-up contract sits beside a payment link and a review option. Clients may like automation but still demand a lawyer's eyes before signing. He tests paid review preference before automating every clause. If human review is the value, automation has to serve that reality rather than replace it in a fantasy.

A leap is not a flaw in the plan. It is the honest place where the plan admits it does not know enough yet. Put the weight there first.

examples.title: Laura Marks the Boot Rental Leap

planSpec.stakes: inventory plans collapse if tourists will not rent instead of buy
planSpec.requiredBeat: Laura marks rental willingness as the business-breaking assumption and tests it first

examples.scenario: At 9:25 a.m. Saturday, Laura straightens a boot rack beside the ski-town hotel door and pins a rental tag under the first pair. The hotel desk card explains the offer, and the deposit amount is still circled on her clipboard. Before ordering more sizes, she must choose whether to test rental willingness first or keep polishing the kiosk setup. The first rental request is the only signal that can justify polishing the tags.
examples.whatToDo: Make rental willingness the first test. Put a small set of boots at the desk, use the deposit amount, and measure whether tourists rent before buying inventory.
examples.whyItMatters: If tourists will not rent boots, the rest of the kiosk plan collapses. Testing that leap first protects the team from perfecting a display for a false belief.

examples.title: Etienne Puts Trust Above Integrations

planSpec.stakes: the model fails if users will not trust automated tax nudges
planSpec.requiredBeat: Etienne puts trust in the riskiest-assumption slot before building integrations

examples.scenario: "The bank link can wait," Etienne says as a calendar alert hovers over a tax folder on the laptop. The trust survey is thin, the manual reminder is ready, and the bank-link mockup is getting all the attention. Before the sprint locks, he has to choose between building integrations and testing whether freelancers trust automated tax nudges at all. The manual reminder lets Etienne test trust before the bank-link build becomes the center of the plan.
examples.whatToDo: Run the manual reminder test before the bank-link build. Measure trust through responses and opt-ins, then decide whether integrations deserve engineering time.
examples.whyItMatters: The model fails if freelancers distrust the nudge. Integration polish cannot rescue a service whose riskiest assumption is that users will accept the advice.

examples.title: Emily Calls the Monthly Payers First

planSpec.stakes: nutrition preferences matter less if adult children will not pay monthly
planSpec.requiredBeat: Emily tests payer commitment before menu variety

examples.scenario: At 11:30 a.m. Thursday, Emily sits at a senior-meal office table with a sample menu clipped to a fridge magnet and the payer call list open beside her. The monthly price is printed in bold, and every recipe conversation feels easier than asking adult children to commit. As program lead, she has to choose whether to approve another recipe cycle or call five payers about monthly payment first. The payer call list makes monthly commitment visible before another menu cycle absorbs the week.
examples.whatToDo: Call the payers before changing the menu. Ask for monthly commitment at the real price, then use the answer to decide whether recipe work is worth expanding.
examples.whyItMatters: Nutrition preferences matter only after the payer leap survives. If adult children will not pay monthly, menu variety is a secondary problem.

examples.title: Pavel Tests the Five-Minute Release

planSpec.stakes: course polish is wasted if supervisors will not release workers for five minutes
planSpec.requiredBeat: Pavel tests supervisor release before filming modules

examples.scenario: You are with Pavel beside the punch clock, where a training tablet sits under the shift roster and a release slip waits for supervisor initials. The HR team wants to film the first safety module this week. Before the camera is booked, Pavel has to decide whether to test supervisor release for five minutes or polish the course script. The release slip is the real gate because training cannot work without five supervisor-approved minutes.
examples.whatToDo: Ask supervisors to release workers for one five-minute test before filming. Treat signed release slips as the first proof the micro-training can reach the floor.
examples.whyItMatters: Course quality is wasted if workers never get access. The release slip tests the assumption that controls whether the rest of the training can matter.

examples.title: Maja Names Trust as the Childcare Leap

planSpec.stakes: matching features fail if parents do not trust reciprocal care
planSpec.requiredBeat: Maja names trust as the leap and asks families for one trial evening

examples.scenario: It took Maja one kitchen-table postmortem to admit the matching features were not the hard part. Printed emergency contacts, a contact sheet, and a two-family cap sat beside the trial evening form. The first parents liked the idea, but trust would decide everything. Maja names trust as the leap and asks two families to try one evening. The trial evening tests trust directly while the matching software remains only a later option.
examples.whatToDo: Test reciprocal trust with one capped trial evening before building matching features. Use emergency contacts and a clear form to make the trust question visible.
examples.whyItMatters: Matching software cannot create trust after the fact. If parents will not try one evening, feature work only decorates a broken assumption.

examples.title: Jack Tests Paid Review Before Clause Automation

planSpec.stakes: automation value fails if clients still demand human review
planSpec.requiredBeat: Jack tests paid review preference before automating every clause

examples.scenario: A marked-up contract lies beside a payment link and a review option on Jack's desk. Before, he planned to automate every clause because clients wanted speed. After three prospects ask who checks the draft, he tests paid review preference first. The next build depends on whether clients choose automation alone or pay for a lawyer's eyes. The payment link tells Jack whether human review is the load-bearing value before clause automation expands.
examples.whatToDo: Offer the review option before automating more clauses. Measure whether clients pay for human review, then shape the tool around the value they choose.
examples.whyItMatters: If clients still demand human review, automation must support that trust need. Testing the preference first prevents Jack from building around the wrong value.

questions.prompt: A team has ten assumptions on a planning sheet before a Monday build review: button color, email tone, onboarding copy, payment trust, and several feature details. Which one should get the first test?
choices: The assumption whose failure would make the current plan collapse.
The easiest assumption to test quickly.
The assumption that produces the most interesting discussion.
questions.explanation: The first test belongs to the assumption with the highest damage if false. Ease and discussion value can distract from the load-bearing risk.

questions.prompt: A boot-rental team is debating tag design and deposit wording at a ski-town hotel before knowing whether tourists will rent boots instead of buying them. What should they do next?
choices: Finalize the tag design so the offer feels professional.
Run a small rental test at the hotel desk with a real deposit.
Order more sizes to make the test look complete.
questions.explanation: Rental willingness is the leap that can break the kiosk. Tag design and inventory matter later if tourists actually rent.

questions.prompt: A fintech team wants to build bank integrations for freelancer tax reminders, but the riskiest belief is whether users will trust an automated nudge before linking an account. Which test should come first?
choices: Build the integrations because trust grows when the product is complete.
Ask the design team to make the reminder screen friendlier.
Send manual reminders to a small group and measure trust, replies, and opt-ins.
questions.explanation: Manual reminders test the risky trust assumption before engineering spend. Completion and friendliness cannot fix a service users will not trust.

questions.prompt: A meal-delivery founder keeps improving menus, but the business depends on adult children paying monthly. Which move handles the riskiest assumption?
choices: Test payer commitment at the monthly price before expanding menu variety.
Survey seniors about their favorite meals before calling payers.
Add more meal photos so the offer feels easier to understand.
questions.explanation: Payer commitment is the dangerous leap for the model. Preferences and photos are useful only after the payment assumption has evidence.

questions.prompt: A manufacturing HR team wants polished training videos, but supervisors may not release workers for five minutes. What is the riskiest assumption?
choices: Whether the videos look professional.
Whether supervisors will make time for workers to take the training.
Whether workers prefer tablets to printed handouts.
questions.explanation: Access controls whether training can happen at all. Video polish and format preference matter only after supervisors release workers.

questions.prompt: A founder proudly shows a long assumption list, then keeps building around the one assumption that scares her most. What is the problem?
choices: She should never list assumptions because lists create fear.
She needs more assumptions before any test is fair.
She has turned assumption work into paperwork instead of steering.
questions.explanation: The list is useful only if it changes test order. Avoiding the frightening assumption leaves the plan exposed where failure would cost most.

questions.prompt: A childcare swap organizer wants matching software, but parents hesitate to leave children with another family. How should she interpret the risk?
choices: Trust is the load-bearing assumption, so one capped trial evening should precede feature work.
Software quality is the safest first test because better matching creates trust automatically.
The idea should be abandoned because trust questions cannot be tested.
questions.explanation: Trust determines whether matching features matter. A small trial can test it directly without assuming software will solve the hardest risk.

questions.prompt: A legal automation tool finds that clients still click the paid human-review option before signing, even after praising automated clause drafting. What does that reveal about the original automation plan?
choices: Clients do not understand technology and should be educated first.
Automation should be shaped around the review value instead of replacing it blindly.
The team should automate more clauses to make human review unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Paid review preference exposes the value assumption. The tool may still work, but its design must follow the trust need clients reveal.

questions.prompt: A team can test a scary payment assumption with five real buyers now or spend two weeks improving a feature users already understand. Which is better?
choices: Improve the understood feature because it will raise confidence.
Do both only after a full investor update is ready.
Test the payment assumption because its failure would make the feature polish irrelevant.
questions.explanation: The payment assumption carries higher damage if false. Feature polish is tempting because it is controllable, but it does not steer the business risk.

reviewCards.front: A plan depends on one unproved belief that would collapse the model if false. What is a leap-of-faith assumption?
reviewCards.back: It is a belief the plan depends on before proof has arrived. If that belief is false, the rest of the work may need to change shape or stop.

reviewCards.front: How do you choose which assumption to test first?
reviewCards.back: Rank assumptions by damage if false. The first test goes to the one that could break the business or make the current plan irrelevant.

reviewCards.front: Why is an assumption list not enough?
reviewCards.back: A list can become paperwork. It matters only when it changes what the team tests first and prevents people from building around the scariest unproved belief.

reviewCards.front: A team keeps polishing safe details. What should you look for?
reviewCards.back: Look for the assumption those details avoid. The safe work may be circling the claim that would embarrass or collapse the plan if tested.

reviewCards.front: Why can testing the riskiest leap feel smaller than building features?
reviewCards.back: The test may be narrow, but it touches the load-bearing belief. A feature build can look bigger while leaving the business-breaking assumption untouched.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to rank assumptions by consequence. The skill is finding the belief your plan cannot survive without, then testing it before safer work absorbs time.

ifThenPlans.plan: If the team has an assumption list, then mark the one that would break the model and schedule that test before feature polish.
If people are debating small details, then ask which unproved belief would make those details irrelevant.
If customers praise the idea, then test the payment or commitment assumption before expanding the offer.
If a process depends on another person giving time or access, then test that release point before building the training, tool, or service around it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tomorrow, choose one active project and write five assumptions. Star the one with the highest damage if false, then define a test that touches it this week.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review whether your current work is testing the riskiest assumption or improving around it. Move one task closer to the load-bearing belief.

memorableLines.text: One belief carries the whole plan: tourists will rent winter boots instead of buying them.
memorableLines.why: It makes the abstract leap visible in the boot-rental scene.

memorableLines.text: Polish should not arrive before the floor is tested.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the chapter's warning against improving around the dangerous assumption.

memorableLines.text: A leap is not a flaw in the plan.
memorableLines.why: It reframes uncertainty as the honest place to begin testing.
